scope: Exact per-call submitted text. Local corrections are not full redesigns; concatenated history is not used for length validation.

calls.submitted_prompt:
Create one original scientific METHOD OVERVIEW for the existing paper "From Forest to Farm: Modeling Nitrogen Dynamics for Sustainable Agriculture" (2025 ICM Problem E). Use case: scientific-educational. This is a source-grounded conceptual illustration for a mathematical-modeling paper, not a popular-science poster, presentation slide, software architecture diagram or set of infographic cards. Generate a new image from the specification below; no existing image is an edit target. All visible text is English.

THE VISUAL ARGUMENT

One shared nitrogen-cycling system is extended from a conserved forest baseline into managed farmland and then into a seven-group food web. The main picture must make the physical carriers, nitrogen pools, feeding relations and targeted interventions visible. A reader should see organisms and a root/soil mechanism before noticing model acronyms. Agricultural management opens the nitrogen budget, changes crop/weed competition and mortality, and supplies alternative model scenarios that are evaluated using the paper's own indicators. The image should feel authored for this particular ecological model, not interchangeable with an unrelated AI pipeline.

Use a compact 3:2 landscape composition with a white ground and scientific natural-history drawing language: controlled ink contours, carefully shaped organisms, restrained local color, short mathematical labels and deliberate connector routing. Aim for a large, high-resolution image with crisp technical lettering. The intended placement is the paper's "Our Work" overview at approximately 180 mm full-text width. The artwork is a raster conceptual draft; do not print claims of publication approval, quantitative validation or native editability. Place the modest title "From Forest to Farm" at the upper left and the small qualifier "Nitrogen-cycle model overview" beneath it. A tiny "Conceptual schematic" marker belongs at the upper right. These headings together take less than one twentieth of the canvas height.

SOURCE AUTHORITY AND NONTRANSFERABLE BOUNDARIES

The authoritative manuscript is the 25-page author PDF for team 2515324. Physical pages 4-8 define the forest nitrogen cycle, assumptions and modified Lotka-Volterra compartments. Pages 9-15 introduce separate crops and weeds, seasonally changing rates, sowing and harvest pulses, chemical mortality terms, and fertilizer input. Pages 16-18 define the seven-group food web, its nine directed feeding links, competition matrix, nitrogen equations and Euler integration. Pages 19-21 compare chemical management, removal of herbicide/insecticide terms, and a separate bat-supported crop-growth extension. Pages 21-22 discuss lacewings, rhizobia/legumes and straw use as additional options; these are not three newly validated simulation treatments. Pages 22-23 examine crop-weed competition sensitivity.

The source assumes species nitrogen content is proportional to population size. Do not silently turn the picture into an empirically calibrated count of individual animals. Individual organisms drawn here are category glyphs. Their illustrative number and size are not abundance or biomass measurements. The forest's total nitrogen is conserved under the stated closed-system assumption. Agricultural inputs and harvest exports break that closed boundary. Do not add atmospheric nitrogen exchange, groundwater loss, carbon accounting or greenhouse-gas pathways to the modeled core: those are not in this model. There is a source inconsistency in the printed forest inorganic-uptake term; this overview follows the explanatory compartment mechanism and the agricultural equations that explicitly use inorganic soil nitrogen. Do not reproduce the inconsistent equation, silently claim to have corrected the simulations, or introduce a second uptake path from organic soil nitrogen to plants.

The paper's nitrogen-turnover quantity is its own stability proxy, not a general proof of ecological stability. Nitrogen input-output efficiency is H/I, not profit and not percentage recovery measured in a field experiment. The denominator includes the paper's modeled inputs including sowing nitrogen, rather than fertilizer alone. No percentage, fitted trajectory, confidence band, bar chart, yield ranking, experimental photo, map coordinate or numerical performance badge should appear. The visual states explain mechanisms and comparisons, not newly generated empirical evidence. The display must not imply that removing chemicals is always better, that bat pollination applies to every crop species, or that the proposed farming options have been tested here.

COMPOSITION: ONE DOMINANT ECOLOGICAL PLATE

Use a notional 1500 by 1000 working grid only to understand allocation; never print coordinates or production instructions. Keep useful content within x=25-1475 and y=22-970. The main managed ecosystem occupies roughly x=340-1120, y=155-770. It is one continuous illustrated food-web and soil scene, not seven node cards and not a decorative landscape. The seven organism groups occupy the air/vegetation portion; an exposed soil section immediately beneath joins roots to the inorganic and organic nitrogen pools. Meaningful organisms, root structure, litter and transfer routes populate this main region. Its objects are substantially larger than anything in the margins.

A small forest-baseline study occupies x=35-305, y=115-370. Below it, x=35-305, y=420-805 holds compact, staggered agricultural operation details. These are open annotations with small concrete objects and local term changes, not two big boxes. A narrow line at the top of the central scene connects the model names as an inheritance annotation. A slim evaluation region occupies x=1170-1465, y=120-770; it contains three scenario definitions, one shared numerical solution operation and the evaluation quantities. The lower area, y=845-955, holds a concise legend under the main mechanism and three small discussion-only farming options at the lower right. This is not a six-panel a-b-c-d-e-f grid. There are no equal-height banners, colored background rectangles, deep rounded cards, thick block arrows or empty footer stripe.

Allocation bounds do not mean drawn frames. Use white space around local labels and arrowheads, but avoid broad empty bands between areas. If a region looks empty, enlarge the nearby scientifically meaningful organism, root system or local process. Do not add a second copy of the whole food web or a generic microscope/leaf/cog icon. Keep outer margins small, internal gutters narrow, and visual mass distributed through actual mechanisms. Open paper-white connector lanes should remain readable; filling every gap with texture or arrows would be wrong. Neither pastel backgrounds nor shadows count as scientific content.

Read from the small forest baseline into the dominant managed food web and open soil budget, then to the scenario assessment. Discussion-only options remain separate from the integrated equations.

MODEL INHERITANCE IS NOT A MATERIAL FLOW

Along y=88-124, above the ecological region, set a compact line reading "FENCM" then "AENCM" then "AE-FW-NCM". Use thin neutral-gray arrows and two short annotations: "add seasonal management" on the first transition and "extend the food web" on the second. Allow unequal gaps based on the main regions below. These are relationships among models. They must not look like broad rivers carrying nitrogen, migration arrows taking an individual forest tree into a crop, or a claim that all three model states occur simultaneously in one geographical field. Place "Forest baseline" with the first acronym and "Managed agroecosystem" near the main scene. Do not print long acronym expansions in the artwork. The full explanation belongs in the external caption.

The final model retains the crop/weed distinction, management and soil/decomposer compartments of the agricultural model. Communicate that retention through one coherent main scene, not by drawing a new disconnected mini-soil under every model. Conversely, do not connect the small closed forest's soil compartment to the farm's soil with a colored material arrow. The closed-system inset and open-system main scene have distinct boundaries, linked only by the gray model-development annotation.

SMALL FOREST BASELINE: A REAL COMPARTMENT MECHANISM

Draw a modest deciduous tree with visible branching, a few understory plants and an exposed small root section, contained naturally by their silhouette rather than a rectangle. Near the vegetation draw a compact pair of generic consumer silhouettes, such as a small leaf-eating insect and a small bird, at a smaller scale than the main food-web categories. These forest animals stand for aggregated consumers, not an exact copy of the farm topology. Label the tree/understory "Producers" and the consumer group "Consumers". A short arrow from producers to consumers shows feeding; do not draw the reverse as a nitrogen gain for plants.

At the base of this small study show leaf litter as "Organic N", a compact microbial-decomposition glyph, and a small clearly labeled "Inorganic N" soil pool. The aggregate route is inorganic pool to producer roots, producer to consumers, producer and consumer returns to organic litter, and decomposition from organic matter back to inorganic nitrogen. Use a small unfilled circular bracket or compact return arc to make the closed cycle legible without enclosing a large blank disk. Label the lower boundary "Closed N budget". Do not draw fertilizer, sowing or harvest inside this forest baseline. Do not show a decorative wide sky, distant mountains, logging machinery, farmhouses or a full painted forest. Every twig or leaf group should help establish the actual biological carrier.

The forest inset is subordinate but well populated by its tree, litter, microbes and uptake route. Keep it aggregate; do not squeeze four tiny predator levels into this inset.

MAIN ORGANISM IDENTITIES AND GEOMETRY

The central baseline food web has exactly seven labeled categories in the manuscript order: "1 Crops", "2 Weeds", "3 Herbivorous insects", "4 Predatory insects", "5 Bats", "6 Birds", "7 Snakes". The numerals identify the source's state-vector indices, not ranks or abundances. Place the labels next to their organisms with compact superscript-like identity numbers or a small aligned prefix; no numbered circular badges large enough to compete with the biology. Labels must remain readable at reduced width, with line breaks only in the two insect labels if needed.

Draw crops as a small cluster of recognizable cultivated cereal-like stems with seed heads, leaf sheaths and fibrous roots. This is a schematic crop category, not a taxonomically fixed experimental crop. Draw weeds as a differently shaped broadleaf/grass cluster with irregular branching and an independently visible root network. Crops and weeds must be distinguishable by morphology as well as green hue. Their plants sit on the same continuous soil surface so competition for shared inorganic nitrogen is spatially plausible. Do not make the weeds a second copy of the cereal crop with a new label. Avoid overlarge flowers suggesting that the baseline cereal glyph is a measured bat-pollinated crop.

Draw herbivorous insects as two or three compact, carefully articulated leaf-feeding insect forms, with distinguishable head, body and legs, positioned above and between crops and weeds. Draw predatory insects as one or two distinct insect silhouettes with a narrow waist or grasping form, not a cartoon ladybug mascot. Their labels carry the scientific categories; the exact illustrative morphology is not a claim about a species. Bats have wing membranes and a compact body, birds have feathered wings and a beak, and the snake has a restrained curved body with a clear head. Avoid smiling faces, giant eyes, glossy plastic surfaces, clip-art stickers or unrealistic biological accessories.

Use the following approximate anchoring to keep the nine feeding paths traceable: weeds near x=455,y=505; crops near x=765,y=505; herbivorous insects near x=605,y=360; predatory insects near x=720,y=235; bats near x=430,y=185; birds near x=895,y=185; snakes near x=1040,y=350. The soil surface begins around y=575, with roots entering it from the two plant groups. Adjust labels around these objects without moving organisms into the right analysis strip. The upper and lateral animals should remain close enough to the central plants that the whole scene reads as one model, not isolated cartoons around a vacant center. Use routes and local biological detail to connect the plate, not a full rectangular shaded background.

FEEDING TOPOLOGY: NINE AND ONLY NINE DIRECTED LINKS

Solid dark-teal arrows mean nitrogen transfer along feeding relations and point from resource/prey to consumer/predator. They are not arrows indicating who attacks whom. Preserve these exact directed links: 1 to 3, 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 3 to 5, 3 to 6, 4 to 5, 4 to 6, 5 to 7, and 6 to 7. This matches the binary predation matrix and Figure 9. There is no crops-to-birds edge, no weeds-to-bats edge, no predatory-insects-to-snake edge, no insects-to-snake shortcut and no snake-to-bird arrow. Do not create a two-headed feeding arrow as a shortcut for two effects.

Use a short upward-left route from crops to herbivorous insects and a short upward-right route from weeds to herbivorous insects. Route herbivorous insects to predatory insects along a short upward-right link. The herbivore-to-bat link can curve around the left of the predatory-insect region; the herbivore-to-bird link uses a distinct outer-right curve. Predatory insects reach bats with an upper-left route and birds with an upper-right route, staying separate from the two direct herbivore links. Bats reach snakes by an upper outside arc with enough clearance above the bird label; birds reach snakes by a shorter downward-right arc. A line crossing another without a dot does not establish a relationship. Wherever possible, prevent crossings by staggering attachment points and using the available exterior lane.

Each feeding arrow ends beside its receiving organism, outside the label. Use consistent thin strokes: width does not encode measured flux. All nine edges must remain traceable, including with the headings hidden.

CROP-WEED COMPETITION AND ROOT UPTAKE

Place a short dark plum line with a blunt T-shaped end at BOTH sides between the crop and weed groups, near the soil surface and below the two upward feeding routes. Label it "Competition" with a small "C" nearby if there is room. The two opposed blunt ends denote reciprocal inhibition represented by the off-diagonal crop/weed competition terms. This is not mutualistic nitrogen exchange. Keep it distinct from triangular feeding arrows. Do not turn the root networks into a complete web of lines; show just enough intersecting territory to make the shared resource meaningful.

Below the plants, the inorganic-soil pool sends two clear upward uptake arrows, one into crop roots and one into weed roots. Roots have fine branches, but the arrows attach to the larger root crown regions so their endpoints remain legible. Add the short label "Root uptake" near the shared branching point. The source growth terms use inorganic nitrogen; no additional arrow should connect leaf litter directly to a producer or make soil organic N look like instantly absorbed fertilizer. Crops and weeds share the pool but retain their own state identities. A root-crossing in the illustration is not a drawn symbiotic connection.

SOIL SECTION: THREE DIFFERENT NITROGEN ROLES

Draw an elongated shallow cutaway immediately beneath the plant groups, approximately x=345-1110,y=570-765. Use a light mineral-soil wash, sparse granular texture, visible fine roots and a few decomposing leaf fragments. The cutaway edge defines a physical soil region, not a pastel dashboard panel. It should not be a huge brown rectangle containing three empty labeled bubbles. Place three meaningful local structures within it: an organic-litter patch labeled "Organic N" near the right side, a magnified microbial colony labeled "Decomposers" near the center, and a small inorganic-nitrogen reservoir/soil-solution field labeled "Inorganic N" to the left, beneath the crop/weed roots.

The core decomposition relation is organic matter consumed by decomposers, a portion retained in decomposer biomass, and a mineralized fraction reaching the inorganic pool. Use an amber-brown arrow from the organic patch into the microbial colony. From that process, a separate mineralization route reaches inorganic nitrogen; label the process "Mineralization". A small return arc from decomposer biomass back to organic matter is labeled "Mortality". These objects correspond to the distinct N_org, N_D and N_inorg states; do not merge decomposers into the organic pool or imply that all organic nitrogen passes quantitatively through microbial biomass before becoming mineral nitrogen.

One thin warm-brown return collector takes source-supported mortality and unassimilated material from the plants and consumer web toward the organic-litter patch. It may be summarized by an unobtrusive bracket under the consumer region with the label "Litter, mortality + residues". It must not collect the harvest export, which leaves the modeled farm. The collector is an explicitly aggregated return path, not a seventh or eighth trophic edge. Do not draw seven long brown lines across the entire food web; use short local leaders into a clearly labeled summary route. The same color is used for the underlying soil decomposition arrows, making the return cycle distinct from the dark-teal feeding links.

Give the microbial detail an actual visual role: a small patch with a fragmented leaf edge and a few bacteria/fungal forms, with a thin unarrowed magnification leader to the soil patch. This is a conceptual local view, not a microscopy image or a fitted microbial community. Do not add a scale bar, taxonomic species labels, bright fluorescent textures or a numeric magnification. Its role is to reveal decomposition rather than provide decoration. Keep the magnification modest enough that the main food web remains dominant.

AGRICULTURAL OPERATIONS: SHOW WHAT EACH CHANGES

The left support area shows concrete management operations in a compact vertical arrangement without equal boxes. Each operation has one target and one short local annotation. Near y=430, show a few seed grains entering a small crop seedling/root glyph, labeled "Sowing". A slim amber arrow points into that crop state, and a short label identifies "crop N input". This is a pulse at sowing, not continuous transfer from the soil organic pool. The operation detail may be a magnified crop fragment; use the same leaf/seed-head morphology as the main crop so its identity is obvious. Do not draw a generic document labeled Input.

Near y=545, show a crop stem with a clear clipping/cut indication and an outgoing small harvested-stem bundle, labeled "Harvest" and "N exported". The arrow starts from the crop and points outward, never from the weed or the soil. The main model removes the harvested crop material, including the fraction retained in straw; the human-food harvest H is a fraction of that removal. For this overview, do not draw a precise fractional split or a pie chart. Keep one correct export and reserve straw reuse for the discussion-only area. Do not connect the main harvest arrow straight back to organic soil as if composting were included in every simulation.

Near y=660, show a modest fertilizer granule/sack symbol with a readable "Fertilizer" label and a short amber arrow that points into an inorganic-soil glyph, labeled "soil N input". Use a local source/target miniature rather than a very long line across the main soil section. A shared label or thin explanatory leader can establish that this is the same kind of inorganic pool as in the main scene. No arrow should terminate on the microbial group or leaves. The paper's fertilizer term, like chemical mortality, is active only while crops are present; do not imply year-round input in an empty field.

Near the bottom of the left support area put two small distinct controls: "Herbicide" aligned with a weed sprig, and "Insecticide" aligned with a herbivorous-insect glyph. Use a blunt-ended plum control mark toward each corresponding miniature and the compact note "mortality terms". An adjacent brace labeled "while crops are present" applies to these controls and the fertilizer input. Sowing and harvest themselves are scheduled pulses, not gated by this same present-crop note. There should be no direct pesticide-to-bat or pesticide-to-snake toxicity edge in the central modeled graph. Although the discussion mentions broader impacts, they are not a license to add unmodeled mechanisms here.

Place a small seasonal cue at the edge of the central plant region: two adjacent leaf/season glyphs and a short alternating pale band labeled "Seasonal rates". If a symbolic wave is used, it has no axis, tick labels or measured values and is clearly a periodic-rate glyph, not a simulated population curve. A short gray association points to the crop/weed growth and mortality annotation, not to the entire forest inset. Avoid cartoon suns and clouds floating over every scene. Seasonality is a parameter modulation in this model; do not add a weather-prediction module, climate-map input, radiation balance or rainfall flux.

HOW THE SCENE ENTERS THE MODEL

Just beneath the soil section, use one compact symbolic statement "Species N + soil N pools" beside a small aligned state-vector glyph. Show seven adjacent ticks labeled only by the already established 1-7 identities and three soil-compartment labels if needed; do not fill it with fabricated numbers or random heatmap colors. It is a representation cue, not an additional algorithm. Pair this with the short text "Coupled nitrogen dynamics". Feeding relations, competition, soil conversion and management are parts of the same coupled model, not four serial processing steps.

Do not print the long full matrix differential equation if it forces microscopic lettering. A compact local "A, B: feeding" and "C: competition" is permissible only if those letters can be read clearly and their neighboring visual relations are already visible. The goal is a model embedded in biological carriers, not an equation placed next to unrelated animal drawings. A single neutral arrow from the coupled-state cue enters the shared Euler-solution step in the right-hand region. It means numerical evaluation of the equations. It is distinct from the colored physical nitrogen transfers inside the ecological scene.

SCENARIO COMPARISON: ALTERNATIVE CONDITIONS, NOT THREE STAGES

At the top of the right region place "Compare model runs". Below it arrange three compact unequal-height rows with no enclosing colored cards. Each row pairs a small target/change sketch with a short condition label. First row: "Chemical management", with the existing herbicide and insecticide controls directed to a weed/insect pair. Second row: "No herbicide / insecticide", with those same control marks visibly absent or crossed out once and the text "chemical terms off". Removing these terms does not imply removing fertilizer, sowing or harvest; do not label this row "No inputs" or show a completely abandoned field.

Third row: "Bat-growth extension", with a bat and a generic crop-growth sprig linked by a dashed plum facilitation arrow, and a compact "+ r₁ᵇᵃᵗ N₅" beside the crop growth-rate label. Use the exact small qualification "scenario only". The bat symbol is the same category as organism 5, but this facilitation relation is outside the baseline feeding network. It is an extension to the crop growth-rate function in Eq. 23, not another prey-to-predator edge, not nitrogen excreted by bats into soil, and not a claim that all illustrated cereal plants are bat-pollinated. This row should not invent an unspecified new chemical schedule; it simply identifies the additional growth term considered by the source.

The three rows are alternative settings feeding ONE shared numerical operator labeled "Euler integration". Use a slim gathering brace or separate short neutral arrows into that operator. Do not connect row one to row two to row three as a sequence, and do not represent their order as an increasing quality score. The central model-state arrow and scenario-condition inputs must meet at this same operator. Small repeated field fragments use the same visual identity; changing abundance, crop height or greenness to suggest a better outcome would introduce unsupported result imagery and is forbidden.

Below the Euler operation show a small time-indexed state notation "N(t)" followed by one short downward route to "Assess". No invented time-series plot appears. Under Assess, place two compact mathematical readouts and one sensitivity cue, aligned as actual derived quantities rather than boxed KPI cards. The first reads "η_IO = H / I" with "N input-output efficiency" underneath. The second reads "μ_N" with "N-turnover stability proxy" underneath. The word "proxy" must remain present and legible. The third reads "Crop-weed sensitivity" beside two short symbolic parameter arrows around the competition mark. These arrows express a parameter perturbation, not measured sensitivity direction or magnitude.

Do not print the paper's numerical percentages; no empirical comparison is required for this overview. Do not draw stars, medals, checkmarks, upward profit arrows, balance-scale winner icons or green success badges beside an alternative. All evaluation quantities arise from the simulated system. None should be connected directly to the original forest illustration as if forests and farms were experimentally randomized trial arms. Keep H distinct from the complete crop removal and I distinct from chemical mortality. A short final label "Inform farm management" is enough to describe how interpretation is used; do not make a giant terminal Recommendation box.

DISCUSSION-ONLY OPTIONS AND THEIR SCOPE

Use a short dashed horizontal boundary near the lower-right portion of the page with the heading "Further options · discussion". Beneath it place three compact, detailed local sketches: a lacewing-like insect beside a pest-bearing leaf labeled "Lacewings"; a legume root section with a few visible nodules labeled "Rhizobia + legumes"; and a small cut-straw bundle beside a decomposing-residue patch labeled "Straw reuse". Their surfaces and anatomy should be understated, precise and recognizably different. Do not put each in a separate equal pastel card. The shared dashed boundary is a scope distinction, not a dashed biological transfer arrow.

Keep these three discussion options outside the coupled model: no rhizobium-to-soil input, no straw-to-soil return and no eighth lacewing node. They are not newly solved scenarios.

Keep the discussion group subordinate, with its scope label readable. Removing it must not break any core-model connection.

VISUAL GRAMMAR, LABELS AND ROUTING

Use a restrained palette: charcoal/navy for text and numerical-model relations, natural muted green for plants, warm mineral browns for soil and organic matter, dark teal for directed trophic/uptake nitrogen routes, amber for external nitrogen inputs/exports, and muted plum for competition/control/facilitation. Physical organisms use plausible muted colors instead of encoding every species with a different saturated hue. Plum blunt ends mean inhibition/control; the single dashed facilitation arrow is restricted to the scenario extension and has its own direct label. Gray model-inheritance arrows never share the physical flow style. The graph needs the legend, but should not depend exclusively on color.

At lower left under the soil mechanism, place a compact line legend using a short solid arrow, a warm-brown return arrow, a blunt-ended competition line and a gray model arrow. The corresponding labels are "feeding / uptake", "organic returns", "competition / control", and "model relation". External N arrows are labeled at their actual input/export locations and need not add another long legend sentence. The scenario-only facilitation is labeled locally. All line samples have equal modest lengths; their labels do not become a title band.

Use one clean scientific sans-serif family and coherent weights, with mathematical variables in a compatible italic style. The main title is compact, local headings modestly bold, species labels regular-to-medium, and short qualifiers smaller but still readable. At full-text width, target roughly 8-10 pt equivalent for primary organism/operation labels and no less than about 7 pt equivalent for the few secondary qualifiers. This is a design target, not a fabricated print-validation claim. Prefer a shorter label or a two-line insect name to shrinking every text item. Do not use typewriter text, oversized all-caps headings, sticker lettering or decorative outlined fonts.

Set labels on clean white space immediately beside their targets. Do not place black type on a dark brown soil patch; provide a small unobtrusive light label clearing without enclosing the whole mechanism in a card. Do not let a line run behind a letter, a wing, a root crown or another arrowhead. Connections that share an actual source can branch with a visible small junction dot; accidental crossings have no dot. Explanatory magnification leaders have no arrowhead, so a microscopic detail cannot be mistaken for a state transition. Keep all arrows in front of the background but clear of organism contours.

Keep the finish a refined ecological mechanism plate, with texture only inside scientific objects. Avoid watercolor splashes, neon highlights, comic shadows and glossy infographic styling.

REFERENCE ADAPTATION AND FINAL CHECK

Borrow selectively from object-rich Sivia reference designs: concrete local before/after operations and precise operand endpoints as in the inspected DiffDock composition, and persistent identity plus local geometry detail as in the inspected Neuralangelo composition. Do not copy their molecule surfaces, rabbits, diffusion networks, SDF fields, training panels, rainbow color maps, seven-column arrangements or repeated cards. The newly reviewed MeshGraphNets reference supports keeping a physical object's identity when a local operation is expanded; no graph neural network, mesh, decoder or learned simulator belongs in this ecological model. GraphCast's multimesh recipe is not scientifically applicable here and must not be imported. The paper's own nitrogen-cycle and food-web figures supply the scientific relations, not their original panel layout or source pixels.

Before completing the image, trace all nine prey-to-predator links, the separate crop/weed inhibitory relation, the two root uptake routes, the aggregated organic-return path, and the decomposer/mineralization relation. Confirm the forest inset is closed while the farm shows external nitrogen input and crop export. Confirm fertilizer goes to inorganic N, sowing goes to crop N, harvest leaves crops, herbicide targets weeds and insecticide targets herbivorous insects. Verify the bat-growth arrow exists only in the scenario row. Verify the three scenario conditions are alternatives into one Euler operation, η_IO reads H/I, μ_N is called a stability proxy, and discussion-only options do not feed the modeled core.

Check the silhouette: the main ecosystem and root/soil mechanism dominate. Tighten vacant margins and enlarge meaningful objects without adding unsupported stages. Render one complete original overview with detailed objects and short labels. The actual output still requires review.

Edit this supplied ecological overview precisely. It is the edit target, not a loose style reference. Preserve its 3:2 canvas, natural-history organism drawings, soil/root detail, compact composition, legible typography, right analysis column and discussion-only lower-right group. Make scientific connector corrections only; do not add new modules or change the visual style. The paper is the 2025 ICM E "From Forest to Farm" nitrogen-cycle model. This request is a local correction of the existing generated image, not a new overview design.

1. REPLACE THE UPPER MAIN FOOD-WEB ARROWS WITH THE EXACT NINE LINKS.

Keep the seven main organism positions and their identities: 1 Crops at lower right of the main vegetation, 2 Weeds at lower left, 3 Herbivorous insects in the center, 4 Predatory insects above them, 5 Bats upper left, 6 Birds upper right, 7 Snakes right. Remove the present dark-teal feeding connectors above the main soil, including the incorrect long bat-to-bird arc and the incorrect herbivorous-insects-to-snake shortcut. Redraw exactly these nine directed solid dark-teal links, with arrowheads at the receiver: 1→3; 2→3; 3→4; 3→5; 3→6; 4→5; 4→6; 5→7; 6→7. Direction is prey/resource to predator, not who attacks whom.

All nine need separate visible origins and endpoints. The predatory-insect group 4 MUST have outgoing links to BOTH bat 5 and bird 6; these cannot silently originate at herbivore 3. The bat's one outgoing edge MUST end at snake 7, not bird 6. The snake receives ONLY bat and bird inputs, never direct insect input. Crops and weeds each feed herbivore 3 only. Do not use unlabeled shared buses for different prey species.

Practical routes: retain the short converging plant→herbivore paths. Put 3→4 on the central short upward lane. Put 3→5 outside the left of the central lane, and 3→6 on a distinct curved lane below/right of predatory insects. Put 4→5 and 4→6 on the short upper left/right lanes with their source visibly touching group 4. Route 5→7 through a high outer arc ABOVE bird 6, continue around the bird without touching it, and terminate at snake 7's upper-right receiving anchor. Route 6→7 down the short right lane. If an arc needs space, move a label slightly, not a species identity. Keep the nine lines the same modest width; there are no numerical flux weights. Preserve the crop-weed blunt-ended Competition link and the correct root-uptake arrows.

2. REPAIR THE ORGANIC-RETURN AND DECOMPOSITION ROUTES.

Remove the brown bidirectional-looking line between crops and weeds below "Competition". It is not nitrogen exchange between the plants. Keep the label "Litter, mortality + residues" and use an unarrowed narrow collecting brace under the biotic scene. From that collector, draw ONE brown return arrow to the right-hand Organic N litter patch in the soil. Route it along the right edge of the soil so it clearly ends on Organic N rather than either plant, a root or inorganic nitrogen. This is an aggregated return from biota, not a quantitative flux and not harvest return.

In the main soil, make the two opposite local paths unambiguous: Organic N → Decomposers as a lower short leftward arrow labeled "Decomposition"; Decomposers → Organic N as a separate upper curved rightward arrow labeled "Mortality". Their arrowheads must face opposite ways and attach to the correct compartments. Retain Decomposers → Inorganic N labeled "Mineralization" as an aggregate process route. Do not merge decomposer biomass, organic N and inorganic N. Do not add direct organic-N uptake by plants. Preserve the two teal Inorganic N→root uptake arrows.

3. MODEL OUTPUT MUST NOT FEED DISCUSSION OPTIONS.

Delete the large gray rightward arrow at the bottom between "Coupled nitrogen dynamics" and the dashed "Further options · discussion" area. No arrow enters that discussion region. Rename the small source annotation over the bottom state vector "Coupled N model". Near the LEFT input of the right-side Euler integration box add a compact local input label with the same wording "Coupled N model" and a short gray arrow entering that box from the left. Use this repeated explicit source label to avoid a long global wire through the soil or discussion group. The model and alternative scenario conditions both feed Euler integration; its output remains N(t)→Assess. Preserve H/I, the nitrogen-turnover stability PROXY wording, sensitivity, and Inform farm management. No numbered result or new chart.
